title: Population Ecology
standard_text: Population size and density; estimating population size by quadrats and mark–recapture; population growth curves (geometric and logistic); carrying capacity and limiting factors; interactions in communities: competition, predation and symbiosis; social organisation; ecological succession. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 2; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 2 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): population size and density, population growth, carrying capacity and limiting factors, interactions between species and population attributes. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support.
body_html:
How to think about it

Population size can be estimated with quadrats (for plants and slow animals) or the mark–recapture method: N = (number first marked × number caught second time) ÷ number recaptured with marks.

With unlimited resources a population grows geometrically (J-shaped curve); in nature, limiting factors such as food, space and disease slow growth, giving a logistic (S-shaped) curve that levels off at the carrying capacity. Organisms interact by competition, predation and symbiosis (mutualism, commensalism, parasitism).

Example

40 marked; later 50 caught, 10 marked. Estimate N.

(40 × 50)/10

Answer: 200

Example

Oxpeckers eat ticks off buffalo. Which interaction?

Both benefit.

Answer: mutualism

Common mistakes

  • Multiplying the wrong numbers in mark–recapture.
  • Thinking a population can grow forever.
  • Mixing up commensalism and mutualism.

faq.a: A factor, such as disease or competition for food, whose effect increases as the population gets denser.

faq.q: Why do predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles?
faq.a: More prey means more food for predators; then predators eat more prey, prey fall, and predators fall after them.
